title: Checking a dose against a stated maximum or dose range
blurb: Compare a prescribed dose or daily total with a stated maximum or range, and work out what can still safely be given.
question: A child weighing 18 kg may have a medicine up to 75 mg/kg in 24 hours. Three doses of 270 mg have been given today. How much more, in mg, may be given in this 24-hour period?

teach.body: Formal rule: maximum = stated maximum per kg × weight (or the fixed maximum given), compared like for like: single dose with maximum single dose, 24-hour total with 24-hour maximum. Plain English: work out the ceiling, add up what has been or will be given in the same period, and look at the gap. The stem always states the maximum; you are never asked to recall one.
teach.cite: FACTS.md section 6 (prescription or protocol always stated in the stem)

teach.h: Worked example: Mia at home with a community children's nurse
teach.body: Mia, 5, weighs 18 kg. Her medicine's stated maximum is 75 mg/kg in 24 hours. Maximum = 75 × 18 = 1350 mg. She has had 3 doses of 270 mg = 810 mg. Remaining = 1350 − 810 = 540 mg. A fourth 270 mg dose (total 1080 mg) stays within the limit.

teach.text: Comparing a single dose with a daily maximum: 500 mg looks far below a 1.5 g/day limit, but 500 mg four times a day is 2 g, which exceeds it. Always multiply up to the same period before comparing.

teach.h: A dose range for a 22 kg child (10–15 mg/kg)
What to do with the result
teach.body: If a prescribed dose or daily total exceeds the stated maximum, do not give it: withhold, check the prescription and contact the prescriber, in line with NMC Code standard 18 (prescribe, supply and administer medicines within your competence and the law). In Part A you only calculate the figure; the clinical response belongs to Part B.

items: Maximum = stated mg/kg × weight, or the fixed figure in the stem.
Compare like with like: dose with dose, 24 h total with 24 h maximum.
Convert g to mg before comparing.

summary: You can now calculate a maximum dose for a person's weight, compare it like for like with single doses or 24-hour totals, and work out how much may still be given or by how much a prescription exceeds the limit.

A.q: A medicine has a stated maximum of 3 g in 24 hours. A person has been given two doses of 1 g in the last 24 hours. What is the most that can still be given in this period, in mg?
A.why: Maximum = 3 g = 3000 mg. Given = 2 × 1000 = 2000 mg. Remaining = 3000 − 2000 = 1000 mg.

whyNot.0: Subtracted one dose instead of two.
whyNot.3: Converted g to mg by × 100, not × 1000.

A.q: A child weighs 14 kg. The stated maximum for a medicine is 60 mg/kg in 24 hours. What is the maximum dose in 24 hours?
A.why: Maximum = 60 mg × 14 kg = 840 mg in 24 hours.

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the weight.
whyNot.1: Divided by the weight instead of multiplying.
whyNot.2: Weight taken as 140 kg, a tenfold slip.

A.q: A medicine has a dose range of 10 to 15 mg/kg per dose. A child weighs 22 kg. What is the lowest single dose within this range?

whyNot.1: This is the highest dose in the range.
whyNot.2: This is the midpoint of the range.
whyNot.3: Weight taken as 220 kg, a tenfold slip.

B.q: A medicine has a stated maximum of 1.5 g in 24 hours. Each dose is 250 mg. What is the largest number of doses that can be given in 24 hours?

whyNot.0: Assumed 6-hourly dosing rather than working from the maximum.
whyNot.1: 1.5 g taken as 15000 mg, a tenfold slip.
whyNot.3: Divided by 300 mg instead of the 250 mg dose.

B.q: A child weighing 20 kg is prescribed a medicine at 20 mg/kg every 6 hours. The stated maximum is 60 mg/kg in 24 hours. By how many mg does the prescribed 24-hour total exceed the maximum?
B.why: Prescribed = 20 × 20 = 400 mg × 4 doses = 1600 mg. Maximum = 60 × 20 = 1200 mg. Excess = 1600 − 1200 = 400 mg.

whyNot.1: This is the prescribed total, not the excess.
whyNot.2: Compared one dose with a quarter of the maximum (100 mg), not the daily totals.
whyNot.3: Counted six doses for every 6 hours.

B.q: A protocol says give 12 mg/kg per dose up to a maximum of 500 mg per dose. A person weighs 45 kg. What dose should be given?
B.why: Calculated dose = 12 × 45 = 540 mg, which is above the 500 mg cap, so the dose given is 500 mg.

whyNot.0: Calculated dose, but it exceeds the 500 mg maximum.
whyNot.1: This is the amount by which the cap is exceeded.
whyNot.2: Weight taken as 450 kg, a tenfold slip.

C.q: A child weighing 16 kg may have a medicine up to 75 mg/kg in 24 hours. Three doses of 240 mg have been given today. How much more, in mg, may be given in this 24-hour period?
C.why: Maximum = 75 × 16 = 1200 mg. Given = 3 × 240 = 720 mg. Remaining = 1200 − 720 = 480 mg.

whyNot.0: Subtracted one dose instead of three.
whyNot.3: This is the amount already given.

C.q: A child weighing 12 kg may have a medicine up to 30 mg/kg/day, given as three equal doses. The oral suspension is labelled 100 mg/5 mL. What is the largest volume, in mL, for one dose?
C.why: Daily maximum = 30 × 12 = 360 mg. One dose = 360 ÷ 3 = 120 mg. Volume = 120 ÷ 100 × 5 = 6 mL.

whyNot.0: This is the whole day's maximum volume.
whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Divided into two doses instead of three.

C.q: A person is prescribed 1 g of a medicine every 4 hours. The stated maximum is 4 g in 24 hours. By how many grams does the prescribed 24-hour total exceed the maximum?
C.why: Every 4 hours = 6 doses = 6 g. Excess = 6 − 4 = 2 g.

whyNot.1: This is the prescribed total, not the excess.
whyNot.3: This is one dose, not the excess.

reteach.title: Same period, then subtract
reteach.question: A maximum is 2 g in 24 hours. 1.25 g has been given. How much more may be given?

blocks.body: Put both in mg: 2000 mg maximum, 1250 mg given. Remaining = 2000 − 1250 = 750 mg. Anything above that in the same 24 hours exceeds the limit.

blocks.text: Comparing one 500 mg dose with a 2 g daily maximum tells you nothing: multiply by the number of doses first.

explain.body: A maximum in mg/kg must be multiplied by the weight: 40 mg/kg/day × 26 kg.

test.q: A child weighs 26 kg. The stated maximum for a medicine is 40 mg/kg/day. What is the maximum daily dose?

whyNot.0: Forgot to multiply by the weight.
whyNot.1: Halved the maximum as if for two doses.
whyNot.2: Weight taken as 260 kg, a tenfold slip.

test.q: A medicine has a stated maximum of 2 g in 24 hours. A person has been given 1.25 g in the last 24 hours. What is the most that can still be given in this period, in mg?

whyNot.0: This is the amount already given.
whyNot.3: Converted g to mg by × 100, not × 1000.

test.q: A person is prescribed 500 mg of a medicine four times a day. The stated maximum is 1.5 g in 24 hours. By how many mg does the prescribed daily total exceed the maximum?
test.why: Daily total = 500 × 4 = 2000 mg. Maximum = 1500 mg. Excess = 2000 − 1500 = 500 mg.

whyNot.0: This is the prescribed daily total.
whyNot.3: Worked out the excess in grams (0.5 g) but gave it as mg.

test.q: A medicine has a dose range of 5 to 10 mg/kg per dose. A person weighs 34 kg. What is the highest single dose within this range?

whyNot.1: This is the lowest dose in the range.
whyNot.2: This is the midpoint of the range.
whyNot.3: Weight taken as 340 kg, a tenfold slip.
